The on-going work presented at ISGC25 Physics and Engineering track and in this article explores
different technical approaches for management and analysis of data obtained from large physics
simulations, with the goal of optimizing data-driven workflows across Cloud-Computing (IaaS)
and HPC systems. The work is connected to research activities on database usage in the context
of High Performance Computing conducted through the EXA4MIND Horizon Europe project.
The case presented here, is a large-scale parameter study of plasma physics simulations carried
out on supercomputing systems at LRZ (Garching b.M., DE). It uses the Particle-in-Cell [4]
code PSC [7], using the FDTD [16] method for electric fields, to simulate the movement of
ionized hydrogen plasma , i.e. protons and the corresponding electrons, in a small (nano- to
micrometer scale) amount of matter (”mass limited target”, MLT) that is driven to very high
energies by irradiation with ultra-intense femtosecond laser pulses. When evaluating the large
amount (approx. 50 TB) of simulation output consisting mostly of particle trajectories, much
work goes into postprocessing and re-assessing the data. This typically happens several times in a
repeating process of varying parameters for processing, like time step selection, cut-off thresholds
and plotting style adjustments. The goal is an integrated and comprehensive methodology to
facilitate such a re-use of the data with an eye on FAIR research data management is our final
objective.

1.
Introduction
1.1 Motivation
Particle-in-cell simulations that model systems of charged subatomic particles are a typical
application making extensive use of the capabilities of high-performance computing (HPC) systems
to simultaneously calculate a large amount of particle trajectories through solving differential
equations for electromagnetic fields on large 3 dimensional grids. The particle and field information
can be written to disk at regular intervals (output steps) during the simulation and the resulting files
fill Gigabytes to Terabytes of storage for each run. In our example, the scientific task is to determine
the optimal set-up for the creation of high energy fast protons that are being emitted by the target.
This acceleration of protons occurs after the laser pulse has delivered its energy onto the plasma,
creating a charge imbalance which gives rise to a strong accelerating electric field. The exact form
of this accelerating field can differ because of shifting dynamics in the relative motion of electrons
and protons during laser-plasma interaction. The particle trajectories contain the momentum data
which can be used to calculate the changing kinetic energies of the particles and thereby determine,
by which mechanism they were predominantly accelerated and how the process can potentially be
fine tuned with optimized laser and target parameters. The production of such simulation output
can take a significant time (weeks to months) of a researcher’s time to first prepare a well-designed
model that fits the scientific question being investigated and then monitor the execution of the runs.
It may consume up to several millions of CPU hours to run the larger simulations. In order to study
the dependency of physical processes on set-up parameters such as target density and laser pulse
properties, these values have to be varied by conducting a parameter study of many simulations
that can be compared for optimal outcome of acceleration processes. These parameter studies then
have to be postprocessed and evaluated in order to reach conclusions that can be used to plan new
experiments.
1.2 Physics background
Ion acceleration with relativistic laser pulses has been intensively investigated in the past years
([2], [8]). The work by P. Hilz et al. [10] showed expanding targets levitating in a Paul trap
as a feasible way to produce sub-solid density targets for ion acceleration, but it remained unclear
whether the pulse parameters and the stage of expansion achieved were optimal. It was hypothesized
that a better coupling efficiency with the laser pulse can be expected for higher areal densities (
comp. [13]). After the simulation model that we developed correctly reproduced the experimental
findings by T.Ostermayr[9], we were confident to use the same model to start exploring optimized
parameters for new Paul Trap experiments planned by P.Hilz et. al.
An illustration of the expanding micro target with electrons being stripped of in the interaction
with the laser pulse is shown in Figure 1.
1.2.1 Simulation Set-Up
We make use of the “Plasma Simulation Code” (PSC, [1, 7]) developed in the group of H. Ruhl
at at the LMU Munich for our simulations.

Target radii are varied between 1.3 𝜇𝑚to 3 𝜇𝑚and initiatlized with different density. The
number of quasi particles per cell is 10 protons and 10 electrons while the number of real particles
represented by one quasi particle is varied to achieve different mass densities.
A Gaussian pulse (at wavelength 𝜆= 1 𝜇𝑚) is seeded into the domain at a distance of 10
microns from the target. The particles are initialized with a Maxwellian momentum distribution
corresponding to a 1 keV plasma temperature.
A rectangular domain of 36 𝜇𝑚× 36 𝜇𝑚× 63 𝜇𝑚and 2304 × 2304 × 4032 cells is used
resulting in a spatial resolution of 64 cells per micrometer. Boundaries are open to allow for seeding
(with radiation reflection at the boundaries below 10 percent). Particles that hit the boundaries are
deleted from the grid.
1.2.2 Data Output
These simulations follow the trajectories of 300 million particles, writing out their properties
and location trajectories at regular time-step intervals (typically 10 to 20 times in one run). They
have traditionally been written to separate HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format v5, [6]) files for each
timestep containing 7 datasets: uid (particle unique id), the momentum values for each particle(px,
py, pz) and the position on the grid (x, y, z) which are stored in separate datasets in HDF5 files(see
Figure 2).
Even for one study, the datasets are revisited typically several times, for example, for visualiza-
tion and comparison against experimental data,. For such purposes, efficient and systematic data

management is paramount.
In industry and administration databases are routinely employed for data that are frequently
reused and are being extended and added to. It is much less common in scientific computing and
especially in the HPC domain. When writing HPC simulation data to permanent storage, there
typically is a need for parallel I/O which is most elegantly done with parallel file access based
on MPI (Message Passing Interface, https://www.mpi-forum.org/) as is possible with HDF5 ([6].
There are often also technical challenges in running a Database Management System (DBMS) server
on HPC cluster nodes or accessing them externally because of, for example firewall restrictions.
However, database systems have many advantages which we will discuss below, which give a
recurring motivation to re-evaluate the benefits of proper data-management methods and systems,
especially for complex parameter scans and warm data that is re-used iteratively. We are also
keeping in mind the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable [15]) which
are an important goal in modern research data management (RDM), striving to add transparency to
research processes and foster better collaboration.
1.3 Benefits of Database Management Systems
Databases have been heavily used, researched, and continuously improved for decades and
have many mature features and sophisticated optimizations that can benefit the management of
complex HPC output data. In this work we focus on SQL type databases (see Figure 3)., which
are well suited for interconnected datasets (relational DB paradigm) containing mostly numerical
data. The primary examples used in our tests were PostgreSQL and MariaDB (MySQL), which
have a long history of widespread adaption since their introduction in the mid 1990s, are free to
use, comparatively easy to install, and well documented. In the following, we list a few examples
of highly useful inbuilt features of these DBMS.
1.3.1 Retrieval Optimizations
There are refined customizable structures like database indexes that help manage and optimize
data retrieval and can enable sub-linear lookup times. These are in some cases created automatically
by the DB system or can be implemented manually by the user.

A common way to enhance database performance that is present in most database implementa-
tions are indexes. For example also PostgreSQL or MariaDB primarily used in our tests, implement
so called sparse indices, bitmaps and b-trees. These potentially help the database server to find and
retrieve specific rows or blocks much quicker than without such meta information, allowing for very
fast filtering of the relevant rows of a data set. However it as to be taken into account that indices can
also add overhead to the database systems’ representation of data, so should be used only when the
relevant filtering operations are expected to be executed frequently. An example would be the use
of a bitmap index to select rows for particle type, which can have only few values, in our example
electron or proton (and occasionally carbon ion), or a sparse index to find data pertaining to certain
timesteps or certain portions of the simulation domain (patches) in a large table.
There is also the option for user-defined functions and re-use of query plans to enhance usability
and efficiency of queries.
1.3.2 Data Updates/In Place Manipulation
Appending additional columns is easy with a single SQL command and can be done in place
(see 7, so information derived during post-processing, such as for example the calculated distance
from a specific point or threshold, velocity or kinetic energy of a particle, can easily be stored in
the same table by adding a column (see Section on Dynamic Data Additions). It is also a very
convenient way to add markers/tags to rows, like selecting particles that are of special interest. An
example in the use case investigated in this work, is the tagging of particles that will reach higher
velocities at a later time in a simulation run. These tags are only attributed to a small fractions of
particles, thus leaving most rows of this ”tag“ column empty. Sparse database columns like these
add very little additional disk space volume to the data as (int contrast to file formats such as HDF5)
it is not necessary to store None or Zero Values as NaN, INTEGER or FLOAT. Instead for example
in PostgreSQL only a single bit per row is used to mark empty fields (comp. [12]).
This approach of adding tags and aggregated values to the corresponding rows eliminates the
need for storing additional files with derived data, like lists of the fastest particles and statistics
about shifts in temperature and density over time. Such additional files increase the complexity of
the data archive as their location has to be managed separately from the raw data. The cost however
is of course a growing size of the main data table, which is a trade-off that has to be considered, if
many additional fields are needed.

1.3.3 Advanced Caching
Typically DBMS applications, like for example the PSQL server, contain multilayered buffering
and caching functionalities (see documentation [11]), which can help speed up queries by 1 to 2
orders of magnitude, when the same data is accessed repeatedly, according to our tests (comp. Fig
8). These are in addition to memory management by the operating system (OS) and can be tuned
in the config files of the database system to avoid overuse of resources, if a server runs on a shared
system, for example when there are several DBs deployed on one machine.

1.3.4 Metadata and Statistics
The inbuilt command ”pg_stats” in PostgreSQL can show information like ”n_distinct” (the
number of distinct values in the column), most_common_vals (list of the most common values
in the column), most_common_freqs (list of the frequencies of the most common values), his-
togram_bounds (list of values that divide the column’s values into groups of approximately equal
population.) Table comments can be used to make notes on simulations of special interest. meta-
data tables can be added to store additional information that can be retrieved by key words and
table relations in contexts when they are needed, like checking for certain parameters or passing on
information about the creator, author and owner of the dataset.

1.3.5 Synchronized archiving
Databases like PostgresSQL (PSQL) have long been deployed in environments where they are
operated in clusters and they contain mature methods to synchronize between different instances.
These can be used to create mirrors and dynamic backups if the data is used from several sources
and by different users and frontends and redundancy is required.
2.
Processing Workflow Requirements
During the simulation, the domain is divided into patches to distribute into the separate MPI
ranks running on different compute nodes. After the initial write-out of particle and field data,
which is done into a separate file per domain patch and output time step in the PSC code, the data
is re-organised into larger datasets via python scripts. This process is a relatively time consuming
intermediate step in the traditional method, often running many hours as a slurm job which opens
the HDF5 files from each rank and creates new datasets from the combined contents. If the data
is stored in PostgreSQL tables, concatenation of sub-sets can be easily achieved via the UNION
SQL-command. It is therefore a valid approach to keep data from different simulation patches
separate for easier management, as many processing operations can be done separately on the data
chunks, and later combined via JOIN SQL statements, when a reduction has been achieved, for
example by filtering out particle that are not of the intended species (often only electrons or only
ions are to be processed) or are in an energy range not relevant to the processing task.
Examples of such processing workflows include extraction of statistical information over par-
ticles or timesteps, calculations of spatial distributions over the domain, like plasma density or the
time evolution of distances between ions and their original position. Such evaluations can happen on
various levels – from whole groups of simulation runs in parameter studies, or for single particle’s
trajectories.
2.1 Dynamic Data additions
Accessing data stored in DB tables allows for manipulating the data in place adding new fields
or rows much faster than if HDF5 files would need to be restructured by creating new datasets and
copying existing data. These data manipulations can be done through scripts using SQL queries via
modules like “psycopg2" or interactively through the Command Line Interface (CLI). One attractive
feature of databases like PostgreSQL and MariaDB is the prompt for interactive usage which we
employed both on cloud machines and running on compute nodes of the HPC cluster using interactive
sessions of the SLURM workload manager (https://slurm.schedmd.com/documentation.html) (i.e.
jobs run with the “salloc" command). It allows for browsing in tables and metadata and creating an
overview with tools like “pg_stats”.
If the user has write permission on the data, they can easily add columns, combine tables, filter
for certain tags or values.

We conducted benchmark tests to compare different set-ups for a PSQL database containing
example data in the form of particle trajectory data retrieved from HDF5 files from medium sized
“Particle In Cell” (PIC) simulation runs (comp. Figure 8 ).
These tests compare the data retrievel rate from to PostgreSQL databases, one external (de-
ployed outside the cluster and accessed via the internet) and one internal (deployed on the cluster).
The “RAM-loaded” column refers to operations on tables which had already been accessed in prior
queries immediately before and the table contents are thus cached. In those cases there may also
be benefit from query execution plans being re-used. This shows the importance of awareness for
caching for optimization of processing of database inputs and outputs. The “Write out” column
shows the result of tests which write the whole data to the local disk (Scratch) on the HPC cluster
as compared to merely writing a small accumulated result (sum of values in the data). This shows
the speed of tasks that have the retrieval of data as the bottleneck and do not require an extensive
output operation, is significantly faster than, when a write out of large chunks to the local disc is
required.
In our tests we found a difference of one (or up to two) orders of magnitude of data retrieval

speed between an externally running database accessed over the internet and one that has the data
residing in the DSS (comp. figure 6) or on the local SCRATCH disk of the HPC system.
The data rate of writing from a local file into the database from HPC compute node was similar
between the internal and external databases. It is a comparable rate as with a benchmark C code
writing data to disk with a single process which was measured to be 47 MBytes/s on the same
system (comp. Figure 8, upper right portion).
This shows that data ingestion into a data base from files can be slow as if it is executed
in a single thread, but retrieval can be very performant, especially if not limited by a restrictive
bandwidth to the outside of the cluster.
4.
Conclusion and Outlook
During the ongoing work we explore how systematic data storage concepts like DBMS can be
employed to improve re-usability and long term data management without sacrificing performance
during processing workflows. We find serveral crucial benefits in using databases as compared to
the traditional approach of manually managing a large and diverse collection of HDF5 files and
processing scripts. However several technical and organisational questions remain open and the
performance analysis and workflow toolbox remains under development at LRZ. The aim is to
mature the system for data (on the 1-100 TB) scale generated by HPC simulations in plasma physics
and develop best practices in the process that can be applied to other use cases as well. Deliberate
metadata management with the aim of incorporating the FAIR principles aims at fostering in-built
sustainability and enhanced reproducibility.
